content: The document titled Guidelines for Efficacy Testing of Spatial Repellents was published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2013 as part of the WHO Pesticide Evaluation Scheme. It provides detailed protocols for evaluating the efficacy of spatial repellents, which are chemical agents designed to reduce human-vector contact by altering insect behavior. These behaviors include movement away from the chemical stimulus, interference with host detection, and inhibition of feeding responses. The guidelines aim to extend existing WHO recommendations for testing household insecticide products, focusing on spatial repellents with inherent properties for public health purposes. The document outlines laboratory, semi-field, and field evaluation procedures for both technical materials and formulated products intended to protect specific spaces (indoor or outdoor) against mosquitoes. It also allows for modifications to assess the efficacy of candidate products against other flying nuisance pests. The term spatial repellency refers to airborne chemicals that induce behavioral changes in insects, leading to reduced human-vector contact. This includes movement away from the chemical, inhibition of host attraction, and feeding deterrence. While many household insecticide products, such as mosquito coils, rely on insecticidal activity (e.g., knockdown and mortality), these guidelines emphasize the evaluation of spatial repellency as a distinct mechanism. The guidelines are designed for use with active ingredients (AIs) that have undergone safety assessments, including inhalation toxicity. Any adverse effects or undesirable characteristics observed during laboratory studies and field trials must be recorded and reported. Products submitted for testing must include material safety data sheets, labeling recommendations, and manufacturer certification of compliance with specifications. Independent physical and chemical assessments may be required before efficacy testing. Laboratory studies are conducted under standardized conditions to determine the inherent properties of the active ingredient and its activity against well-characterized mosquito strains. These studies measure movement away from a chemical stimulus, interference with host detection, and feeding inhibition. Specific objectives include establishing dose-response relationships, determining effective dosages (ED50 and ED95), and evaluating the efficacy and duration of protection of formulated products. Testing should be conducted with three or more local anthropophilic mosquito species, such as Aedes aegypti, Culex quinquefasciatus, and Anopheles species (e.g., An. stephensi, An. gambiae). Mosquitoes must be reared under standardized conditions to ensure reliability and reproducibility of data. These conditions typically include a temperature of 27 ± 2°C, relative humidity of 80 ± 10%, and a 12-hour light/dark photoperiod. Assays should be performed on female mosquitoes that are nulliparous, of uniform age (preferably 5–8 days post-emergence), and actively host-seeking. The spatial repellency assay involves a modular test system with a central clear cylinder connected to two metal test cylinders (one control and one treatment). A chemical gradient is created between the two ends, and mosquito movement is observed. Serial dilutions of the active ingredient are tested to identify the effective dose range. The assay is typically performed under static airflow conditions in a chemical hood, with groups of 20 female mosquitoes introduced into the test environment. All test chambers and instruments must be properly cleaned and decontaminated after each test. Blank assays should be conducted to check for contamination before subsequent tests. The inclusion of a well-characterized active ingredient as a reference or positive control is highly recommended. Environmental conditions (e.g., temperature and humidity) during testing must be reported. The guidelines emphasize the importance of good laboratory practices, quality assurance, and adequate training for personnel involved in testing. Standard operating procedures for data processing, management, and validation should be used, and all study staff should have access to these procedures in relevant languages. Data reporting must be of sufficient quality to allow comparisons of efficacy across multiple evaluation sites. The WHO acknowledges the contributions of experts and institutions involved in developing these guidelines, as well as the financial support provided by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation. Feedback and suggestions for improvement are welcomed from national programs, research institutions, and industry stakeholders.
